segments.text: Here at Refund Retriever we are constantly improving our refund technology software to
get the maximum amount of late delivery refunds from FedEx and UPS.
Guaranteed service refunds (GSR) are available when the carrier delivers a package even 60
seconds late.
We try to automates every step in the process.
From downloading invoices to disputing late deliveries, but many times there are roadblocks
that prevent automation from being 100% effective.
Recently a client emailed us with a list of denied FedEx disputes that we submitted.
They were concerned because all the refunds we submitted were denied.
This year we implemented a filter that catches these late FedEx packages that were denied
a refund credit.
Once we see the denial, our system populates another list and our in-house phone dispute
agents call FedEx customer service to have the refunds processed.
It is a time consuming process but our client are seeing more refunds each week.
We logged in to their FedEx online billing, found the invoice, went to the invoice history.
In the invoice history we are able to see total amount due, total amount of payments,
and total number of credits and closed disputes.
Upon investigation we were able to see all the denied disputes.
We looked at the dispute information on the FedEx online billing history to view the reason
for the denial.
FedEx denied the dispute because there was an exisiting payment on file.
There's a 15 day time limit to get refunds for late ackages we were within these 15 days.
Our client had paid for the invoice as soon as it was available.
This caused FedEx to automatically deny any GSR service failure requests.
A call was placed to the FedEx customer service center and our phone dispute agent was able
to get refunds on all 5 of these late packages.
Initially FedEx automatically denied the initial refund requests but our recently implemented
steps paid off and we saved this customer $98.42 on an invoice that originally would
have cost $4253.53.
This is a 2.3% savings.
Withoiut these individual phone calls being made this client would've received 0 refunds
on this FedEx invoice.
Since 2006 we have been trusted by shippers to lower shipping costs.
Does your auditing company take these extra steps?
Refund Retriever does and our clients' always benefit.
Contact Refund Retriever today if you have any questions.
Have a great day!

Parcel Shipping Audits

Most companies are unaware that they are often overcharged for shipping services. Companies receive their monthly bill consisting of hundreds of pages of shipping invoices and have difficulty attempting to review for errors. Our Parcel Audit Program audits a company’s parcel costs via their primary carriers; usually FedEx and UPS.

Objective decisions require objective data, and with our solution, that’s where it all starts. We connect our trusted and proven cloud-based software to your client’s parcel accounts in minutes, importing their electronic invoices from your client’s carrier and extracting critical data to help identify savings opportunities. With this data in hand, you’re clients are able to make objective decisions about their parcel shipping costs—and we’re able to request refunds to recoup those costs.

The process is quick, simple, and requires no work on your clients part—and since your client is only billed based on a percentage of refunds secured, it’s no risk to your client. Your client has access to your online carrier account, we’re able to easily and quickly connect our proprietary software, automatically importing invoices and identifying possible refunds based on a multi-point audit including late deliveries, invalid surcharges, incorrect dimensional and weight charges, and more.

Recouping parcel costs isn’t about placing blame—it’s about holding parcel carriers accountable to their promises. And that’s how Data helps your client. Our process is so simple that we’ll be auditing your client’s invoices by end of day.

In addition to the savings generated by the refunds, clients save, on average, 11% of their annual FedEx/UPS spend through our optimization without switching or changing a thing.

We find clients monthly savings. This program is a month-to-month engagement however it is so highly effective that it has over a 90% client retention rate.

metadata.title: What is the Medicare Shared Savings Program?
metadata.author: Advisory Board
metadata.shortDescription:
https://advisory.com/research/health-care-advisory-board/primers/shared-savings

The Medicare Shared Savings Program—created as part of the Affordable Care Act—is bringing population health management to Medicare patients through a new delivery model called an ACO.

segments.text: The Medicare Shared Savings Program, created as part of the Affordable Care Act,
is bringing population health management to Medicare patients through a new delivery model called an ACO.
But what is an ACO? An accountable care organization is a group of health care providers —
so hospitals, physicians, maybe even post-acute providers — who are collectively responsible
for the cost and quality of care a particular set of patients receive over time.
Physicians choose to be a part of an ACO, and those physicians have their own patients.
And that link, ACO to physician to patient, is how Medicare assigns patients to the ACO.
If — over the course of the year — a patient gets most of their primary care
from physicians in a particular ACO, then that ACO is going to be responsible
for the cost and quality of the care they receive.
And that means all the care — even from providers outside of the ACO.
Once an ACO has its patients, how does it get paid?
Under shared savings, providers in an ACO treat a patient, then bill and get paid by Medicare.
Nothing new there. The big difference is that on top of that normal payment,
the ACO can earn a bonus payment based on the cost and quality of the care patients receive.
But there’s a catch. First they have to qualify for the bonus.
When the ACO signs up for the shared savings program, Medicare looks at the historical cost
for patients treated by the ACO, and then sets a savings target based on that cost.
So if treating a patient at the ACO cost $10,000 before, Medicare could tell the ACO
they have to treat the same patient for less than $9,800 this year to get their bonus.
Each year Medicare will look at all their data and adjust that target based on national trends.
The idea is to get the ACO to focus on controlling cost growth over time.
At the end of the year, Medicare looks at how much it spent on patients assigned to the ACO
and compares the actual spending against the target. If the ACO was above the target?
No bonus. In fact, if the ACO missed the target by too much,
Medicare could actually demand they give back some of the money they’d already paid out.
But if the ACO meets or exceeds the target, then they qualify for a bonus.
In essence, Medicare will share the savings back with the ACO.
If the ACO qualifies for the bonus, how much will they actually get?
To figure that out, Medicare looks at the quality of the care the ACO delivered.
So if an ACO sacrifices quality to cut costs, Medicare isn’t going to reward them for that.
The combination of savings and quality ultimately determines if this bonus is big or small.
The bonus payment comes with few strings attached — the ACO can pretty much spend it however they want.
That’s shared savings in a nutshell.
Dollars are tied to patients, patients are tied to physicians, and physicians are tied to ACOs.
But as you might expect, the devil’s in the details. And the Medicare Shared Savings Program is complex.
Visit advisory.com to see the Advisory Board’s collection
of best practices, research, tools, and expert insight.

metadata.title: How ACO Conveners Are Changing the Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP) Behind the Scenes
metadata.author: Health Affairs
metadata.shortDescription:
Health Affairs Publishing’s Rob Lott speaks to Adam Markovitz of the University of Michigan about his recent paper exploring the growing role of third-party firms in Medicare ACOs ( https://www.healthaffairs.org/doi/10.1377/hlthaff.2025.01574?utm_medium=podcast&utm_source=a+health+podyssey&utm_campaign=june+2026+issue ), highlighting how they have contributed to wider participation and more geographically dispersed networks while raising questions about how these structures relate to shared savings outcomes.

Order the June 2026 issue of Health Affairs ( https://www.pubservice.com/backissue/subbi.aspx?CO=PJ&PC=HR&BI=HRI&utm_medium=podcast&utm_source=A+health+podyssey ).

Sign up for our free Health Affairs newsletters ( https://share.hsforms.com/26dGfZSq8SjaPUznLYa3kfQnnawj ) to stay up to date on health policy news and analysis.

A Health Podyssey
Episode 270
June 23, 2026

★ Additional episodes: https://www.healthaffairs.org/podcasts

Um that they genuinely improve care. Better analytics, better care management, better quality of care. And that's how they lower spending. And to at least get at that, we looked at whether these dispersed conveners actually had the highest quality performance in the MSSP. But we we didn't see that. So the dispersed convener ACOs scored no better on quality on overall quality metrics than the local ACOs or the non-convener ACOs. So they they may have been delivering better care but didn't show up uh in sort of those aggregate quality measures. The second is actually reverse causality. So it's just simply basically the best ACOs that succeed and then they expand over time. They grow into new markets and then they look dispersed. Uh and in that story, dispersion is really a marker of success and not a cause of it. And because ours was a cross-sectional study, um that, you know, certainly is a real possibility that that may be driving some of our findings. And then the third story I think is is the bad one of strategic selection. So that's where conveners are deliberately constructing networks to beat spending benchmarks, cherry-picking low-cost clinicians from across the country regardless of whether or not those clinicians share any patients or are actually doing anything to subsequently reduce spending. >> [snorts] >> And you know, while the convener firms are not advertising this, there is a huge cottage industry of ACO consultants, ACO actuaries whose entire job it is to do exactly this and they are not subtle about it. So, I think the clearest example is a tool called Milliman's ACO Builder, which is essentially a tool for cherry picking low cost doctors. So, they went out, bought Medicare claims data on every physician nationwide, mapped out who's high cost and who's low cost, and then they sell you that map so that you can just grab the low cost ones and build your network to be like as they say on their website structured for maximum performance and shared savings. So, to test whether or not that was happening, we basically built our own ACO builder, but in reverse. So, we took each ACO's patients and asked a simple question, how does their spending compare to other patients in the same county because that's the regional benchmark. And if you've recruited low cost clinicians, your patients should look unusually cheap relative to their local peers. Um and that's exactly what we found. So, the dispersed convener ACOs had the lowest spending relative to the region of any group, roughly $400 below the regional benchmark. While the dispersed non-convener ACOs had the highest, only about $100 below. Again, this is cross-sectional, so this could also reflect subsequent savings that the ACOs did uh generate. Um but you know, one thing to note is like the firms selling tools like ACO Builder, they're not even in our study. So, we could only identify sort of the formal conveners who actually run ACOs, and list themselves as um the ACO executive or the public contact for the ACO in the public files, but there's this entire layer of analytic consultants that's essentially invisible to us researchers and I think to CMS. And these consultants are not coy about what they're doing. So in that sense I think our paper is to some extent the tip of the iceberg. But once you start looking for it it's really it's really everywhere. And I think most most of us so I will say as an academic researcher when I speak with policy makers I think most people still picture ECOs as like these local ECOs who are not sophisticated enough to cherry-pick or game benchmarks like this. And honestly I don't think a lot of them are. But you don't you don't have to be. You don't need your hospital's head of pop health to know how to do this. You just need them to know someone who does and hire them. And I do think that's exactly what they're doing. Like if you spend 10 minutes on LinkedIn uh as I do now and it's wall-to-wall consultants actuaries advertising the software hosting webinars on you know there's a new ACO lead program and like every day people are posting about you know how you should structure your ACO for maximal savings. Um so I think there is this whole industry that is hiding in plain sight. It's just not the mental model that we as researchers have been bringing to these programs. >> Uh remind me to uh connect with you on LinkedIn after this uh >> [laughter] >> Would be a pleasure. >> So your findings highlight this tension right? That's what we're talking about here today between sort of the benefit of increased participation made possible by third-party conveners uh versus maybe this potential undermining of the program when bonuses are achieved through network optimization in theory as opposed to actual coordination and quality improvements. And I'm curious you alluded to some of the entities in the in this ecosystem being invisible to CMS. Do you have a sense of to what extent all of this is on CMS's radar and how the agency has navigated this tension as it's made changes to various ACO models over the years? >> Yeah, and I think that's exactly the right way to frame it because it it is a real tension. You know, so the same firms that do lower the barrier to entry for like these small practices and make it easier to really, you know, improve quality and lower spending. They're also the same firms that make it easiest to win without doing anything. I do think this is definitely on CMS's radar. You can I think read it right off of some of the recent ACO design choices. Um so like for instance just thinking about ACO reach. So that's the the ACO model that lead is now replacing in this coming year. So reach really was CMS's push sort of like in the convener sense. There it was their push to try to reach these small and rural practices that MSSP had left behind. It even opened the door for private firms to directly contract with CMS for the first time in traditional Medicare. You know, there's not been much empirical work on reach yet, but our own preliminary data show that reach ACOs are doing some of the same things we found in in MSSP selecting these low-cost clinicians. And with lead you can you can read some of the the design choices I think as a direct response to some of those concerns. So I I again in my free time as one does, I've read through large portions of the RFA and now they actually ask they have a a question about who runs your ACO and there is a check box for conveners. I've not looked through MSSP's RFA so maybe they did before, but to me that was noteworthy. And in terms of how lead is designed to curb selection, they are now starting ACOs on a pure historical benchmark rather than a regional one. So you're measured against your own past instead of being rewarded simply by finding uh cheap clinicians relative to their local peers. And also like in in MSSP, but not in REACH, they require the whole practice to participate. So, unlike in REACH, you can't sort of cherry-pick individual low-cost doctors. Uh and then they actually in their RFA explicitly ban conveners from uh TIN swapping. Uh which means where you basically shuffle the same practice between your ACO. So, they say that if a practice is in an ACO run by a convener and they leave that ACO, they can't join another convener uh another ACO run by that same convener for 3 years. So, clearly they are seeing something in their data in REACH or in MSSP that they're concerned about. Um and they have all this stuff about like uh curbing risk coding. They want to use AI infer A- Aledin talks about AI infer inferred risk scores, which is basically built on objective signals like prescription fills rather than the diagnosis codes entered by by the doctor. >> Mhm. >> Um you know, at the same time I think there's a bigger point and it is why I'm skep- skeptical that any of this will fully or even adequately solve the problem. You know, some of these are are genuinely I think really good ideas. Um but the real big tension here, it's it's not one loophole. This is a volun- all of these are voluntary programs and they're all built on benchmarks and any benchmark can be gamed. And the voluntary part of that makes the benchmarks even the most problematic. Because to get people to join, you have to make it attractive. And people only join if they think they can make money. So, you can never really tighten down the rules all the way without losing the participation that the program depends on. And then the final vicious loop is that every single rule that you add to try to stop gaming makes the program more complex. And the more complex the program gets, the more the doctors and the hospitals need a third-party firm to navigate it for them. If you look at who runs these convener firms, many of them used to work for CMS. They used to work for CMMI. They are specifically the people who know the rules the best. And once you're out of government, of course you would go run a consulting firm about the program that you helped create. And of course, if you are a small practice struggling to make ends meet in fee-for-service, and you want to make money from value-based payment, of course you would contract with a consultant. So, to some extent, this is everyone just acting rationally. But, I think it's ended us in a really difficult spot. You know, so I think that's that's sort of where we've where we've left off. >> Well, uh a difficult spot, but perhaps a glimmer of hope that uh we might be able to continue learning about these conveners and continue studying them uh with uh researchers like Dr. Adam uh Markovitz and his colleagues uh who've really done interesting, important work with this paper. Uh I encourage our listeners to check it out in the June issue of Health Affairs. Dr. Adam Markovitz, thanks so much for taking the time to chat with us today. Really enjoyed it. >> Thank you. Yeah, it's really been a pleasure. >> And to our listeners, thanks for tuning in. Uh if you're a rational actor, you might recommend this podcast to a friend or review, uh and of course uh tune in next week. Thanks, everyone. >> [music] >> Thanks for listening. If you enjoyed today's episode, I hope you'll tell a friend about the Health Policy.

In this video, Dr. Dan Mingle explains proposals for the Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP) in 2026. 
#healthcare #medicare #valuebasedcare

Want to know more about Mingle Health? Visit our website: https://minglehealth.com/

We Ease the Burden of MIPS Reporting:
We’ve streamlined your MIPS reporting to help you mitigate the penalty and succeed with the Quality Payment Program. Learn more about our MIPS solutions here: https://minglehealth.com/products-services/mips-solutions/

APM Performance Pathway and ACO Reporting:
 In the 2021 Final Rule, CMS announced the new APM Performance Pathway (APP) which is now required for MSSP ACOs. In addition, 2021 is the last year for the web interface mechanism. The good news is the new QPP participation option reduces the number of measures from 10 to 3 and aligns the reporting process more closely with MIPS, which many providers and practices are familiar with. APMs with multiple EHRs or different workflows across member organizations will likely face challenges in their ability to aggregate data for their ACO reporting. Mingle Health is here to help. We work with you holistically to meet your goals and bring together data, review workflows, and analyze quality measures. Learn more about our ACO and APM Solutions here: https://minglehealth.com/products-services/aco-apm-solutions/

metadata.shortDescription:
Webinar Title: A Practical Guide to Co-Management/Gainsharing/Shared Savings Arrangements and CMS’s Episode-Based Payment Initiatives

Programs and arrangements that compensate physicians for their work improving quality and reducing cost can benefit everyone involved, including hospitals, ASCs, physicians and patients. 

This session, presented on March 11, 2020, describes the legal issues for potential stakeholders – including medical professionals, medical device companies, and conveners/administrative entities – to consider in designing, implementing and participating in these programs.

It also offers a brief overview and a few practical observations about participation in some of CMS Innovation Center’s Episode-Based Payment Initiatives, including Bundled Payments for Care Improvement Advanced (BPCI Advanced) and the Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement Model (CJR).

Presenters:
Marguerite J. Ahmann
https://www.fredlaw.com/our_people/marguerite_j_ahmann/

David M. Glaser
https://www.fredlaw.com/our_people/david_m_glaser/

metadata.title: Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP) Changes in 2025
metadata.author: Mingle Health
metadata.shortDescription:
In this clip, Dr. Dan Mingle provides an overview of the important changes to the Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP) in the 2025 Final Rule. 
#healthcare #valuebasedcare #medicare #aco 

Want to know more about Mingle Health? Visit our website: https://minglehealth.com/

We Ease the Burden of MIPS Reporting:
We’ve streamlined your MIPS reporting to help you mitigate the penalty and succeed with the Quality Payment Program. Learn more about our MIPS solutions here: https://minglehealth.com/products-services/mips-solutions/

APM Performance Pathway and ACO Reporting:
 In the 2021 Final Rule, CMS announced the new APM Performance Pathway (APP) which is now required for MSSP ACOs. In addition, 2021 is the last year for the web interface mechanism. The good news is the new QPP participation option reduces the number of measures from 10 to 3 and aligns the reporting process more closely with MIPS, which many providers and practices are familiar with. APMs with multiple EHRs or different workflows across member organizations will likely face challenges in their ability to aggregate data for their ACO reporting. Mingle Health is here to help. We work with you holistically to meet your goals and bring together data, review workflows, and analyze quality measures. Learn more about our ACO and APM Solutions here: https://minglehealth.com/products-services/aco-apm-solutions/

metadata.title: Updates to Medicare Direct and Medicare Shared Savings Programs
metadata.author: COPE Health Solutions
metadata.shortDescription:
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) has announced updates to the Medicare Shared Savings Program (Shared Savings Program) and Medicare Direct Contracting models due to the Covid-19 public health emergency (PHE), both of which require immediate action. These updates include an imminent deadline, as early as next month, for Shared Savings ACOs to submit voluntary elections to extend their agreements, as well as a new Letter of Intent opportunity and application period for Medicare Direct Contracting.

The webinar will discuss these opportunities, related action plans, and critical success factors for providers seeking to participate in these and other value-based payment (VBP) programs. We will also explore how these opportunities can fit into an organization’s overall VBP and risk insurance/reinsurance strategies to support downside risk mitigation, both for the remainder of 2020, as well as planning for 2021 and beyond.

Speakers include:
• Andrew Snyder, MD, COPE Health Solutions, Principal & Chief Medical Officer
• Brent Hardaway, COPE Health Solutions, Principal
• Christina Mendez, Aon Reinsurance Solutions, Senior Managing Director,
National Managed Care Leader

Utility bill audit service shows if your company is due a refund from any utility company nationwide. http://goo.gl/kk3TLO Receive a free utility bill analysis. No obligation for a free utility bill audit consultation.

No out of pocket expenses to you. If our Utility Bill Audit Examiners can't find you a refund or savings, we don't get paid. 

Did you know that your utility company wants to make as much money from you as possible? Of course you did, but did you know that you can get the same exact service you are getting for your company now, for less?

Less than 10% of all billing errors, overcharges, and saving opportunities are discovered and reported to utility providers. As for refunds, if you think these large utility firms are simply going to hand you a check for overages you've paid, think again.

Let our utility bill auditing specialists help identify these over-payments and find your company monthly savings on your utility bills. The refunds alone can often add up to thousands of dollars. Ongoing savings can reduce your bill by sometimes as much up to 30% per month and we have real testimonials to prove it. 

This is how it works. After we perform the audit, we will dispute and negotiate with your utility providers to secure all possible savings from refunds and the monthly savings we have identified.  Once the savings have been realized, this money can be used immediately and put right back into your business or simply in your pocket.

For our services, there is no out of pocket cost to you. It's Simple: We get paid out of the savings we provide. If we can't find savings or refund, we don't get paid. However, we find that three out of five companies we work with save money.  What we provide is a truly risk-free proposition that will add value to your organization for years to come. 

We work with both large and small businesses, churches, residential communities, and government agencies.  Whether your organization is a bakery, a church, a manufacturing company, an assisted living facility, or a sewer and water district - we can probably save you money.  

Again, there's no out of pocket expense to you so you have nothing to lose. We are a performance based business which means if we can't find you savings, we don't get paid. 

Our primary focus for the past 15 years has been assisting organizations, just like yours, in the identification and capture of real savings on your utility bills such as electric, natural gas, telecom, water, sewer and other fuel bills.

Ask yourself this, what could your organization do with the extra cash flow every month? 

To get started, Simply submit your information using the contact form provided at http://utilityauditservice.com and one of our utility bill auditors will contact you faster than you expect.

metadata.title: Commercial property tax appeals
metadata.author: LawFull
metadata.shortDescription:
Are you considering filing a commercial property tax appeal? Check out this video for answers to some frequently asked questions about appealing your taxes.

Hey everyone, welcome to the LawFull channel. My name is Barry Zlotowicz and I’m an attorney in Chicago. This is a great place to get answers to your every day legal questions so if you haven’t already please subscribe to my channel. And if you have any questions, put them in the comments section.

Today I’m with Chicago real estate attorney Fred Agustin. So, the first question is, is appealing your property taxes a federal or state issue? It’s a state and even municipal issue. We’re in the state of Illinois so make sure you check your state and jurisdiction for the laws where you are.

So we’re talking about commercial property real estate property tax appeals. When you say commercial property what are you talking about? 
On the residential side, commercial properties could include multi unit residential buildings and condominiums. On the commercial property side, it could include retail, office buildings and industrial properties.

On the residential side, multi unit residential buildings and condos are assessed at 10 percent of their fair market value in Cook County. The commercial properties are assessed at 25 percent of the fair market value.

There are many different ways to appeal your property taxes. These include

A. Market Value: for market value you want to get an Appraisal Report either a full appraisal report or limited appraisal report.

The full appraisal involves three approaches to value:
1. Cost approach
2. Income approach
3. Sales comparison approach

A limited appraisal will only look at the sales comparison approach.

B. The second way to appeal your property is based on an income analysis. This is for properties that are leased. You are analyzing the income that the property produces and you come up with a cap rate to come up with the valuation.

C. The third way under market value is by looking at recent sales. It has to be an arms-length sale. But note that the recent sale is only good for one year and Cook County will reassess in the next year

D. The fourth way is to assess by vacancy. If you have an income producing policy and it’s vacant, if you are trying to get tenants you can get a partial assessment which is also good for only one year.

How do you appeal a condominium’s property taxes? The condo owners should appeal as a “group.” Meaning, as an association or the majority of condo owners should appeal together. The County is going to try and come up with a valuation of the whole building so appealing as a group is optimal.

So where do you appeal property taxes? There are 2 “levels” where you can appeal. The first is at the Cook County Assessor’s office or the Cook County Board of Review – or, you can appeal at both at the same time.

If you’re not happy with the review, you can appeal on a second level which is at the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board (PTAB) or you can file a lawsuit in Cook County Circuit Court.

Finally, you can appeal your property taxes every year in Cook County. This is different than the assessment which occurs every three years. But again, you can appeal your property taxes every year.

If a commercial business is making the same profits as last year, nothing needs to be done. BUT when that commercial business is going through hard times their property taxes don’t change UNLESS some action is taken. 

If Profits and earned revenue for a business has been reduced down, they need to conduct a business property tax appeal. Why? Because business property taxes are based on an income called the INCOME METHOD and if you don't appeal, nothing changes.

Considering the inefficiencies of government, not only for the financially stressed could benefit from a consultation for a basic overview but especially businesses who have been hit hard by revenue shortfalls. 

Using commercial business property tax calculator methods, business property tax appeals are where the big contingency commissions lie. Considering the many businesses that have seen a lack customers, that audience is HUGE! 

Instead of valuating a business using a market value approach, the method for establishing the valuation for a business is based on an Income Approach. Businesses are valued by the income they receive.

At their expense and time, your client’s accountant will supply you with all the important information to solidify your case. You’ll only need to find the client … restaurants, strip malls, hotels, gyms, bars etc. … and they abound everywhere in the present financial climate … and we will furnish you the training

This is exactly the environment where property tax appeals produce results.

metadata.author: Brach Eichler LLC
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of the Brach Eichler Talks Podcast, we discuss why now may be the right time for commercial property owners and net lease tenants to consider a 2026 New Jersey commercial property tax appeal.

We cover the upcoming New Jersey tax appeal deadlines, how shifts in assessed-to-market value ratios may create opportunities to reduce real estate taxes, and why properties located in revaluation or reassessment towns may warrant a closer look. We also explain Brach Eichler’s no-cost, no-obligation review process and available fee arrangements.

📲 Read the full alert now at https://www.bracheichler.com/insights/now-is-the-time-to-consider-a-commercial-property-tax-appeal-2026/

metadata.title: Cost Segregation Example: $750K Commercial Property Tax Savings (2026)
metadata.author: CostSegRx
metadata.shortDescription:
Can a $750,000 commercial property generate more than $100,000 in accelerated depreciation?

Brian Kiczula of CostSegRx walks through an estimated cost segregation benefit for a small commercial property purchased for $750,000, using tax year 2026 and 100% bonus depreciation.

The example starts with the property’s baseline details:
• Purchase price: $750,000
• Land allocation: 20% or $150,000
• Depreciable purchase basis: $600,000
• Additional improvements: $75,000
• Total basis reviewed: $675,000

Based on the estimated cost segregation results, the example shows:
• $101,250 in accelerated depreciation
• $108,003 in estimated first-year depreciation

Brian also reviews the revised fixed asset schedule and explains how the property basis is broken into categories such as:
• Building basis
• Distributive trades and services
• Land improvements
• Land

The estimate also illustrates potential tax savings at different effective tax rates.
At a 24% effective tax rate, the example shows estimated tax savings of approximately:
$25,921

The video also compares trailing depreciation:
• With cost segregation: $14,711
• Without cost segregation: $17,307

This helps demonstrate how cost segregation can accelerate deductions into earlier years while changing the amount of depreciation available in later years.
If you own a commercial property, office building, retail space, warehouse, self-storage facility, or other investment real estate, a cost segregation study may help identify assets that qualify for shorter depreciation periods and potential bonus depreciation.

Want to know what the numbers could look like for your property? Don’t guess, find out.
Request your free Estimate of Benefits and review the results with your CPA or tax professional:
https://www.costsegrx.com

Still have questions about Form 3115? Check out:
https://www.3115wizard.com/

#CostSegregation #CommercialRealEstate #BonusDepreciation #AcceleratedDepreciation #CostSegregationStudy #RealEstateInvesting #CommercialProperty #Depreciation #TaxStrategy #RealEstateTaxes #TaxSavings #CostSegRx

Disclaimer: This video is for educational and informational purposes only and should not be considered tax, legal, accounting, or investment advice. Tax laws and regulations are subject to change, and the benefits of cost segregation and depreciation strategies vary based on each taxpayer’s individual circumstances. CostSegRx does not guarantee any specific tax savings or outcome. Always consult with your CPA, tax advisor, or other qualified professional regarding your specific situation.

Unlock Hidden Savings Without Sacrificing Quality! 
In today's fast-paced business landscape, cost reduction is a critical priority. But while many organizations focus on financial expenses, there's a significant area often overlooked: technology.

🔍 Do Not Exclude a Technology Audit when Looking at Cost Reduction. 🔍

We are excited to share a recent conversation between Stephen Payerle II of Next Level Technologies and Jim Lichtenberg of Schooley Mitchell. These two industry leaders have discovered powerful synergies that help businesses save on costs without compromising IT services and support for office employees and remote sales teams.

Businesses should request a technology audit alongside a financial expense and services audit. This dual approach uncovers hidden savings and optimizes both financial and technological resources. 🗳 📝 💰 ✅ 

Steve and Jim have a track record of proven strategies to help companies achieve substantial cost reductions while maintaining a high-quality tech stack.

🎥 Watch the short clip to discover how Next Level Technologies and Schooley Mitchell can transform your approach to cost reduction. 👀

metadata.title: The Waste Audit Process: step by step guide
metadata.author: Pacific Regional Environment Programme (SPREP)
metadata.shortDescription: Waste Auditing is a fundamental activity that is used to understand waste management practices and enable national governments to understand and respond to the social and environmental issues posed by waste management. Undertaking auditing in a standardised process enables governments to track trends over time and make informed decisions on systems and processes.  This animation provides a summary of waste auditing and introduces resources to assist with audit design and planning.

segments.text: Every day we create waste at home, at
work, at school. But do we really know
what we're throwing away? Understanding
what wastes we are generating can help
us make smarter decisions for a cleaner
community.
A waste audit helps us understand how
much waste we generate, the type of
waste generated, how much of it could be
reused, recycled, or avoided all
together. This structured approach
provides the foundation for improving
waste management systems.
By measuring and analyzing waste over
time, we can gather valuable data to
inform actions to improve our waste
management systems.
Key benefits of conducting a waste audit
include identifying specific waste types
of interest and action. Identifying any
emerging waste issues and opportunities
would generate
reporting. Evaluating the performance of
existing waste systems. Identifying
opportunities to reduce costs.
Identifying the need for additional
waste infrastructure to support a
growing and changing household,
business, or community. With vibrant
economic growth across the Pacific,
waste volumes and types continue to
evolve. Accurate and relevant data is
essential to inform national
decision-making and to design effective
waste management programs and services.
Waste audits can be undertaken at
various scales. Household audits
assesses domestic waste generated by
families. Commercial audits examine
wastes from businesses and offices.
Landfill audits capture materials
collected through waste collection
systems and dispose at landfill.
Customs audits help forecast future
waste by analyzing imports. Stockpile
audits measure waste stored in central
locations.
Effective planning is the foundation of
a successful waste audit. Start by
selecting your audit team. The group
should include individuals with the
right expertise and understanding of the
waste audit process. The team will be
responsible for collecting, sorting,
weighing, and recording waste data
accurately.
Develop a clear waste audit plan.
Outline the audit's goals, the types of
materials to be assessed, the timeline,
and the specific data to collect. Ensure
that health, safety, and risk management
protocols are in place, including
assessing risks and implementing
mitigation measures. Procure all
necessary personal protection equipment
or PPE to ensure the safety of your team
during the audit. Before beginning the
audit, conduct comprehensive training to
your audit team on the audit processes
and safety protocols. oversee and assist
the team to ensure proper handling and
sorting of wastes, minimizing the risks
of injury and ensuring hazardous
materials are managed appropriately.
Ensure the team sort collected waste
samples, weigh and record results in
approved data collection templates.
Enter the data collected from the field
into the audit spreadsheet to support
accurate analysis and evidence-based
decision-making. Accurate data recording
is critical. All data entries must be
reviewed and verified to ensure
completeness and reliability
using waste audit results. Waste trends
can be determined, future needs
predicted, and more effective waste
management strategies developed.
Recognizing the importance of waste data
collection, pack waste plus a regional
program funded by the European Union and
implemented by spre supported Pacific
Island countries and team Oolstee in
collecting waste data to support
national decision-making.
The pack waste plus program's regional
data framework identified key
performance indicators relevant to
informing waste trends in the region and
provided guidance on collection of data
utilizing evidence-based decision-making
for a cleaner Pacific.
[Music]

Act one: in lots of our videos we talk about concepts such as improving your recycling rate or using more recycling services.

This is all great - but to be honest is a little bit theoretical. And as we all know - theory does not always meet well with reality.

So - in today's video - we will look a bit more at the dirty work. How do we know how much recyclable material is actually in your bin - and if your business is making real progress in recycling more - and sending less material to landfill.

Let's talk about a waste audit.

Act 2 - 

The concept of a waste audit is pretty simple - it means to perform a formal analysis of the content of your bins.

We often like to estimate what we throw out - but there is no comparison to actually getting in the bin - and really finding out.

In broad principles - a waste audit involves selecting a bin (that should be the one you want to test - or broadly representative) - hopefully when full etc.

You then basically empty the bin on to the ground and separate the waste into categories - i.e. such as :

cans
cardboard
food waste
or whatever else is appropriate to your business.

Of course - this work will be dirty - and involve opening waste bags etc.

This type of work is generally done by companies specialising in this type of work - such as waste consultants. It is dirty work - and can also be hazardous - as there can be broken bottles, unexpected items like syrynges - and getting into and out of a large bin can be tricky - so best leave to someone who knows what they are doing. Protective clothes, boots and gloves are a must.


Act 3 -once this is done - you can have a really good analysis of what actually goes in the bin - and from there - implement improvements such as better recycling processes or even a new recycling bin.

The old saying is - if you can not measure it - you can not improve it. A waste audit that tells you you have 50% recylable materials in your general waste bin - will open up lots of opportunities for improvement.

If you did the same style audit next year - you should really see an improvement.

For lots more recycling info - visit us at waster.com.au - and like and subscribe below.

metadata.title: Understanding shipping surcharges
metadata.author: FedEx APAC
metadata.shortDescription: Wherever your package is headed, the base rate and fuel surcharge are predictable. Other fees might not be as obvious, but with a little know-how you can avoid surprises. With the right tool and knowledge, you are in control. Learn more at fedex.com.

segments.text: Understanding shipping surcharges
Wherever your package is headed
the base rate and fuel surcharge are predictable
Other fees might not be as obvious
but with a little know-how you can avoid surprises
The common fees fall into two categories:
Shipment-related surcharges and Customs clearance-related fees
To learn more
please visit the Surcharge and other information page
To stay in control
always provide accurate shipment details during booking to calculate applicable surcharges from the start
For example
ODA and OPA surcharges apply when your shipment travels to or from remote or
less-accessible locations outside standard service zones
Before shipping
check the ZIP and postal code list by tier to see if ODA or OPA applies
And when possible
consolidate deliveries to optimize costs
An Non-Standard Shipment Fees may be applied if your shipment meets specific criteria such as dimension
weight and packaging
For details, visit this page
Always provide accurate weight and dimensions when booking
and pack your items securely using appropriate materials
The packing guide is a great resource to help you pack with confidence
Accurate shipment information helps ensure precise rate estimates
Now
let's talk about customs-related fees
which are often undetermined during booking due to varying customs clearance processes
For example
a storage fee may apply when shipments remain uncleared by customs beyond the allowed time
To avoid these fees
ensure all documentation is complete and accurate to help expedite customs clearance
Another example is disbursement fees
which apply when FedEx pays duties and taxes on your behalf for timely shipment delivery
For assistance with customs-related fees
visit this page
Additionally
the FedEx Global Trade Manager tool helps review customs document requirements and estimate duties and taxes
enabling you to avoid delays and prepare for potential charges
Staying informed helps you stay ahead
With the right tool and knowledge
you are in control
Learn more at fedex
com

metadata.title: Extra shipping charges explained | Fees, duties and surcharges
metadata.author: FedEx Europe
metadata.shortDescription:
Your shipment is sent and the invoice has arrived – but what exactly are you paying for? 

In this video, we explain the most common surcharges like duties, taxes, fuel, processing, special handling, dangerous goods, remote delivery and address correction, so you'll know what to expect.

0:22 What am I paying for? 
0:40 Duties and taxes 
1:18 Processing fees 
1:39 Carrier surcharges 
2:00 Fuel surcharge 
2:17 Special handling 
2:35 Dangerous goods 
2:48 Delivery to remote areas 
3:08 Address correction

Learn more about extra shipping charges: https://www.fedex.com/en-gb/how-to/calculate-costs/what-extra-charges-can-be-added.html

For more videos like this, visit 'How to ship' at fedex.com: www.fedex.com/howtoship

segments.text: Hi, and welcome to this video about carrier surcharges.
Have you ever sent a package
and ended up paying more than expected for the shipment
or did your online order arrive with an additional payment request?
In this video, we take a look at the most common surcharges
and discuss who should pick up the bill.
What am I paying for?
If you need to pay additional fees,
there are three types of extra charges you could be billed for,
duties and taxes, processing fees, and carrier surcharges.
Let's take a closer look at each of them.
One, duties and taxes.
Duties and taxes are fees related to import and export regulations.
They can be added to the total price at checkout
or charged by customs when your parcel enters a country.
Here's how it works.
Your carrier will prepay the fees and will ask the sender or the receiver
to reimburse the costs.
Some carriers will send a payment request to be paid before they deliver goods.
For online purchases, the seller's website or checkout page will usually mention
who needs to cover these costs.
Two, processing fees.
If your carrier takes care of customs clearance
and the initial payment of duties and taxes,
all you have to do is pay the bill when it comes.
A fee for doing the work on your behalf
will appear on the same invoice as the duties and taxes for your shipment.
Three, carrier surcharges.
Carrier surcharges are also sometimes called service costs,
administration charges, or disbursement fees.
They cover anything that falls outside of the standard shipping price.
Usually these costs are charged to the sender.
Let's take a look at the most common ones.
Fuel surcharge.
Oil prices fluctuate continuously, and that affects fuel prices.
The fuel surcharge is a fee added on top of the basic shipping price
that helps your carrier cover these changing costs.
Special handling.
When you're shipping goods that are fragile, oddly shaped,
or exceed your carrier's standard dimensions,
they'll need to be handled separately.
It's a bit like getting extra legroom for your goods,
so expect to pay more.
Dangerous goods.
If you need to ship goods that potentially pose a risk to a person
or other shipments, they'll be handled as dangerous goods
and will also incur additional charges.
Delivery to remote areas.
Planning to send something to a remote island?
If your carrier doesn't have a regular service to that territory,
they may still be able to deliver your package.
Keep in mind that you may be charged an extra fee for that extra mile.
Address correction.
Typos can be pricey,
especially when your carrier needs to adjust the paperwork for you.
Luckily, you can easily avoid this surcharge,
just check, check, and double check.
That's all about the most common carrier surcharges.
Thanks for watching!
For more videos like this, visit ‘How to ship’ at fedex.com
and start shipping with confidence.

segments.text: In this video, we’ll show you how to fill in a commercial invoice.
It's important to complete your commercial invoice correctly, to lower the risks of delay.
The invoice should preferably be printed on paper with a company letterhead.
It must include your company details,
such as the address, contact details and tax number.
You’ll also need to include the same details about the receiver.
First, fill in the shipping date and number.
The shipping number is sometimes known as an Air Waybill.
Next, state the reason for export. Why are you sending it?
Is it for example for trade or is it a gift?
Don't forget to state the correct Incoterm.
This determines who's responsible for the package during shipping.

metadata.title: How to Measure a Box for Shipping | The Official FedEx Guide
metadata.author: FedEx
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn how to measure a box for shipping with this official FedEx step-by-step guide. Accurate package dimensions can help you avoid unexpected shipping charges, delivery delays, and dimensional weight pricing issues. In this video, we'll show you how to correctly measure the length, width, and height of a shipping box, explain why package size matters, and share tips to help ensure accurate shipping rates and smooth delivery. Whether you're a small business owner or an occasional shipper, mastering box measurements can help make shipping easier and more cost-effective.

Whether you're a small business owner or just sending a gift, understanding how carriers determine shipping costs is essential. Learn how to find your box's length, width, and height, calculate dimensional (DIM) weight, and check for oversize limits using the length and girth formula. Getting it right prevents surcharges and keeps your shipments on track.

CHAPTERS
• 0:00 - Why Accurate Measurements Matter
• 0:22 - How to Measure Length, Width & Height
• 0:43 - External vs. Internal Dimensions
• 1:08 - How to Calculate Length + Girth for Oversize Rules
• 1:29 - What is Dimensional (DIM) Weight and How to Calculate It
• 2:15 - Final Tips to Avoid Shipping Problems

👇 Key Formulas Mentioned:
• Length + Girth = Length + (2 x Width) + (2 x Height)
• Dimensional Weight (U.S. & International) = (Length x Width x Height) / 139

Avoid the hassle of returned packages and surprise charges. Follow these expert tips to pack and ship with confidence.

For more packing guides and resources, visit:
➡️ FedEx How to Pack: https://www.fedex.com/en-us/shipping/packing.html

Need a hand? Our experts are ready to help pack and ship for you at a FedEx Office location near you.
➡️ Find a FedEx Location: https://local.fedex.com/

metadata.title: UPS Large Package Surcharge for 2025
metadata.author: Refund Retriever
metadata.shortDescription:
Many shippers are surprised when they open their weekly UPS invoices and find a large package surcharge applied to specific shipments. To help control shipping costs, we’re taking a closer look at this surcharge—what it is, how much it costs, and strategies to mitigate it.

What is a UPS Large Package Surcharge?
For domestic shipments, UPS applies a large package surcharge when:
-The length (longest side) + girth [(2 × width) + (2 × height)] exceeds 130 to 165 inches, or
-The package length alone is between 96 and 108 inches.

What is the Cost?
-Large packages are subject to a minimum billable weight of 90 pounds.
-If the large package surcharge applies, an additional handling charge will not be assessed.

metadata.title: Sales and Use tax refund requests- Manage your expectations
metadata.author: Sales Tax Sisters
metadata.shortDescription:
When filing a sales tax refund remember that State taxing authorities review refund requests to confirm they are valid.  This is true regardless of whether you file a separate claim for refund or if you make adjustments on your sales and use tax return.  If you make an adjustments per your sales and use tax return, you must be able to prove the adjustment is valid, if you are ever audited.

When making a refund request or making adjustments per your sales tax return, review the website of the applicable taxing authority to ensure you have all documentation that fully supports the request. Want to unlock major tax savings and boost your short-term rental cash flow? Start with AirDNA’s STR tools today! https://bit.ly/4odKwrA

Are you overpaying taxes on your Airbnb income? Discover how the cost segregation strategy can transform your biggest expenses into powerful tax-saving opportunities. In this video, we break down exactly how short-term rental owners can use cost segregation to accelerate depreciation, reduce annual tax bills, and reinvest faster into their STR business.

We explain:
What a cost segregation study is and how it works
Why STRs (short-term rentals) are uniquely suited for this tax strategy
How you can reclassify assets like furniture, appliances, and landscaping to depreciate them over 5–15 years instead of 27.5
Real-world examples of hosts using cost segregation to increase ROI and fund upgrades like hot tubs and designer interiors

Cost segregation isn’t just for large investors—it’s for any serious host looking to scale smarter, reinvest strategically, and build long-term wealth with vacation rentals. Don’t let hidden tax advantages go to waste!

accelerate depreciation on certain
components of your property like

process typically includes three steps.

what qualifies. Next, engineers conduct

early tax savings.

suited for cost segregation. Why?

amenities to stay competitive. From
designer furniture to top tier
appliances, these are all assets that
qualify for accelerated depreciation.

is so competitive, investors have to
reinvest frequently to stay ahead, cost
segregation unlocks cash sooner,
allowing you to fund renovations,
marketing, or even additional
acquisitions, all while staying tax
efficient. If you're reinvesting
regularly to keep your Airbnb listing
top-notch, this strategy is tailor made
for you.

are hard to ignore. Major tax savings
from accelerated depreciation reduce
your annual tax liability. More cash
flow means you can reinvest your
short-term rental faster, whether it's
upgrading a bathroom or installing a hot
tub. Improved ROI helps build wealth and
expand your portfolio. Better guest
experience leads to more bookings and
higher ratings thanks to upgraded
amenities paid for with tax savings. And
perhaps most importantly, it helps
protect you against risk by building a
financial cushion to handle the
unexpected. In short, it's not just
about saving money. It's about gaining
the flexibility to run your business

metadata.shortDescription:
Cost segregation can front-load years of depreciation into one return — if your property and income profile fit. We'll tell you straight whether it pencils for you:
👉 https://www.prosperlcpa.com/apply?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=yt-q326-costseg

Cost Segregation: The Strategy High-Income Earners Can’t Ignore

Cost segregation is one of the most powerful tools in real estate tax planning. By accelerating depreciation, you can unlock massive deductions—sometimes 20–30% of a property’s purchase price in year one. That means keeping more money in your pocket and less going to the IRS.

In this video, you’ll learn:
• How cost segregation works and why it creates immediate tax savings.
• When to use it—long-term rentals, short-term rental loopholes, and more.
• How investors offset W-2 income, business profits, and capital gains with this approach.
• Why top earners and real estate professionals rely on it to reduce taxes and grow their portfolios.

If you’re a business owner or real estate investor, this isn’t just about saving on taxes—it’s about building long-term wealth and protecting your cash flow.

For a personalized opportunity report showing how cost segregation could save you money, visit https://www.ProsperalCPA.com/opportunityreport . To learn foundational tax planning concepts, get our free Ultimate Tax Planning Checklist at TaxPlanningChecklist.com

metadata.title: Cost Segregation After a 1031 Exchange: Depreciation & Timing Rules — I1031 M6 V2
metadata.author: Asset Wise Institute
metadata.shortDescription:
A 1031 exchange does not end when the replacement property closes. That is where the next layer of tax strategy begins.

In this lesson, we explain how cost segregation, depreciation setup, placed-in-service timing, carryover basis, new basis, passive activity limits, and future exit planning may affect the replacement property after a 1031 exchange.

You will learn why investors should not assume the full replacement property purchase price is depreciated like a normal purchase, why land and building allocation matters, how exchange basis and additional new basis may need to be tracked, when cost segregation may help, when deductions may be limited, and why placed-in-service timing can change when depreciation begins.

This video is for real estate investors, landlords, high-income professionals, and advanced 1031 exchange students who want to understand how the replacement property fits into a larger tax strategy.

Related resources:

1031 Exchange Worksheets, Calculators, and Investor Planning Tools:
https://www.etsy.com/shop/ProDeductions?ref=seller-platform-mcnav&section_id=55164999

ProDeductions Digital Products:
https://prodeductions.etsy.com

Cost Segregation Course:
https://www.udemy.com/course/cost-segregation/

AssetWise Institute:
https://assetwiseinstitute.com

Disclaimer: This video is for general education only and is not tax, legal, financial, investment, or 1031 exchange advice. 1031 exchange rules, depreciation rules, cost segregation rules, passive activity rules, and bonus depreciation rules depend on your specific facts and may change over time. Consult your qualified intermediary, CPA or tax advisor, attorney, lender, and financial advisor before making any tax, legal, investment, or exchange decision.

segments.text: Cost segregation, depreciation, and
timing after a 1031 exchange.
A 1031 exchange helps you keep more
equity invested, right? But, what
happens after you buy the replacement
property, right? That is where a lot of
investors stop planning too early. They
think, "I completed exchange. I deferred
the gain. I'm done." But, you are not
done. You are only you have only moved
into the next layer of tax strategy.
Because now you have a new property, a
new depreciation schedule, maybe new
debt, maybe new improvements, maybe
higher income, and maybe a cost
segregation opportunity.
And if you do not set this up correctly,
the exchange might work on paper, but
the tax strategy after the exchange may
be weak.
So, in this lesson, we are going to talk
about three things, right? Depreciation
after a 1031 exchange, cost segregation
after a 1031 exchange, and timing.
Because timing can change when your
deduction
actually start.
So, let's start with depreciation. So,
depreciation is a tax deduction you get
for the wear and tear of the
income-producing property over time.
For a residential rental property, the
building is generally depreciated over a
long period. For non-residential
commercial property, the building is
generally depreciated over an even
longer period. So, here's the important
part, right? Land is not depreciated.
Only the building and some property
components are depreciated. So, even in
a normal purchase, you do not simply
depreciate the full purchase price. You
have to separate land from building.
After a 1031 exchange, here is another
layer. You might not have a completely
refreshed basis.
Part of your basis is a replacement
property
may carry over from the property you
gave up, and part of your basis may be
new basis because you traded up and then
cash added jet or bought a more
expensive asset.
Think about it this way, right? Let's
say you sell an old rental property for
The adjusted tax basis in the property
is only 350k, right? Because you owned
it for years and took depreciation. Then
you exchange into a replacement property
for 2.1 million.
From investor's point of view, you
bought a 1.2 million property.
But from tax depreciation point of view,
you might not get to simply depreciate
1.2 million like a brand new cash
purchase, right?
Your tax professional has to separate
the exchange basis from the additional
new basis and that matter.
Because the old basis might continue
under one set of depreciation rules and
the new additional
basis might have an own depreciation
treatment.
So the question is not just what did I
buy? The better question is what tax
basis did I carry into this property and
what new basis did I create?
That is why after an exchange
depreciation setup is not just
bookkeeping, it is tax architecture.
If the depreciation schedule is wrong,
it might not hurt you today, but it can
hurt you later when you sell, exchange
again, refinance or do estate planning
or trying to explain the numbers to a
CPA.
Now, let's bring in cost segregation.

metadata.title: Cost Segregation Example: $350K Rental Property Tax Savings (2026)
metadata.author: CostSegRx
metadata.shortDescription:
Can a $350,000 rental property generate nearly $50,000 in first-year depreciation?
Brian Kiczula of CostSegRx walks through a real-world style Estimated Benefit example for a Sarasota, Florida rental property acquired for $350,000 and placed in service on July 15, 2026.
The example starts by removing a 25% land allocation, since land is not depreciable.
That results in:
• Purchase price: $350,000
• Land allocation: $87,500
• Depreciable basis: $262,500
Using a 100% bonus depreciation rate for tax year 2026, the estimate shows approximately:
• $46,200 in accelerated depreciation
• $49,806 in estimated first-year depreciation
Brian also reviews the revised fixed asset schedule, including:
• Building basis
• Distributive trades and services
• Land improvements
• Land
• Total property basis
The example also shows how bonus depreciation and current-year depreciation work together to arrive at the estimated total first-year depreciation.
Estimated tax savings are then illustrated using different effective tax rates. At a 24% effective tax rate, the example shows estimated tax savings of approximately $11,953.
The video also compares trailing depreciation to help show how accelerating depreciation may affect deductions over time.
A CostSegRx free Estimate of Benefits can help property owners and their CPAs evaluate the potential depreciation opportunity before deciding whether to move forward with a full cost segregation study.
Think your property could have a similar opportunity? Don’t guess. Find out.
Visit CostSegRx.com and request your free Estimate of Benefits to see how much depreciation your property may be able to accelerate.
Request your free estimate today:
https://www.costsegrx.com
Still have questions about Form 3115? Check out:
https://www.3115wizard.com/
#CostSegregation #CostSegregationStudy #BonusDepreciation #AcceleratedDepreciation #RentalProperty #RealEstateInvesting #SarasotaRealEstate #Depreciation #TaxStrategy #RealEstateTaxes #CostSegRx

metadata.title: 179D Energy-Efficient Commercial Buildings Deduction for Not-for-Profits
metadata.author: Cherry Bekaert
metadata.shortDescription:
179D Energy-Efficient Commercial Buildings Deduction for Not-for-Profits

Section 179D Energy-Efficient Commercial Buildings Deduction (section 179D) is an energy tax deduction created to incentivize the adoption of clean solutions in commercial buildings. Originally intended for the commercial industry, not-for-profit organizations are now able to take advantage of this notable tax deduction if they invest in energy-efficient improvements. 

Since not-for-profits are tax-exempt, they can allocate the energy tax incentive to a taxpaying entity working on the structure renovations. Before applying for the Section 179D tax credit, it’s imperative to understand the solutions that make the most sense for your building and the potential deduction allocations you may be eligible to receive. 

Host Amy Dosik, Not-For-Profit Tax Practice Leader at Cherry Bekaert, is joined by special guests Martin Karamon, Tax Credits and Incentives Advisory Leader, Ed Vettel, Tax Credits and Incentives Senior Associate, and Andre Kohn, Energy Tax Credits and Incentives Senior Associate. Together they discuss the Section 179D energy efficient commercial building deduction and how not-for-profits and schools can benefit.. 

As part of Cherry Bekaert’s Not-For-Profit podcast series, and the second episode in the energy tax credits and incentives mini-series, this episode covers:
Section 179D background
Determining eligibility for Section 179D 
Section 179D benefits 
Enhanced deduction requirements
Maximizing Section 179D opportunities

Cherry Bekaert’s Energy Tax Credits and Incentives team assesses the eligibility of your organization to receive business energy tax credits and incentives, so you can receive the maximum monetary benefit allotted. If your organization makes investments in clean energy advancements, then you may benefit from energy efficiency federal, state and local energy tax credits and incentives. If you have any questions specific to your needs, Cherry Bekaert’s Not-For-Profit group is available to discuss your situation with you.

metadata.title: Understanding the 179D Deduction for Building Designers
metadata.author: Mitchell Tax Law - Texas Tax Attorneys
metadata.shortDescription:
This video discusses the implementation and interpretation of the Sec. 179D tax deduction, which is a tax incentive provided by Congress to encourage energy-efficient commercial buildings. The video uses the Johnson v. Commissioner case to address questions about when the building is placed in service and the amount of the deduction that can be allocated to the designer of the building. The video explains that the maximum amount of the deduction to be allocated is the cost incurred by the owner to place the energy-efficient property in service and the requirements for obtaining the deduction. It also discusses the impact of this deduction on tax-exempt entities and the importance of following the guidelines provided by the IRS.

metadata.title: Form 7205: A&E Firms' Guide to Claiming Section 179D
metadata.author: Cherry Bekaert
metadata.shortDescription:
When the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) was signed, it greatly increased the benefits of the Section 179D Energy Efficient Commercial Buildings Deduction (Section 179D) for A&E firms. A large part of the process when claiming the Section 179D deduction relies on keeping strict documentation. Form 7205 is a form in the claiming process that qualified businesses and individuals use to calculate the deduction, mark yourself as the designer or building owner, and provide information on the person performing the certification and completing the allocation.

The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) released an updated Form 7205 in February 2023. In today’s Professional Services podcast, Cherry Bekaert leaders Scott Duda, Professional Services Industry Leader, and Ron Wainwright, Tax Credit & Incentive Advisory Partner, discuss:

  •  Background on Form 7205
  •  Form 7205 benefits for A&E firms
  •  Impact of the IRA on A&E firm eligibility for Section 179D benefits
  •  Requirements to qualify for Section 179D benefits
  •  Form 7205 requirements
  •  Form 7205 utilization
  •  Future focus areas for A&E firms in 2023

Related Guidance:

  •  New IRS Form 7205 for Returns Requiring Section 179D Documentation (https://www.cbh.com/guide/articles/new-irs-form-7205-for-section-179d-deduction/) 
  •  How Can A&E Firms Take Advantage of New Tax Credits in the Inflation Reduction Act? (https://www.cbh.com/guide/podcasts/inflation-reduction-act-and-its-impact-on-ae-firms/) 
  •  What the New Audit Technique Guidelines Mean for Cost Segregation (https://www.cbh.com/guide/podcasts/new-audit-technique-guide-for-cost-segregation-explained/) 

Learn more about how we help our Professional Services Clients:

metadata.title: 179d Energy-Efficient Commercial Building Tax Deduction Updates
metadata.author: Engineered Tax Services
metadata.shortDescription:
Since the passing of the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022, the 179d tax deduction has been updated so that owners of commercial buildings or residential buildings four stories or more and designers of buildings owned by non-taxable entities can receive a benefit 5 times greater. This video explains the two additional requirements in order to receive the higher benefit.

Is your building project eligible for a tax deduction 5x larger than in previous years?

The Section 179D Energy Efficient Commercial Building Tax Deduction recently underwent a massive "facelift" following the Inflation Reduction Act. For properties placed in service in 2023 and beyond, the potential savings have skyrocketed from $1.88 to over $5.00 per square foot.

In this technical breakdown, we explain the new "sliding scale" for energy efficiency and the specific labor requirements—Prevailing Wage and Apprenticeship—that act as the gatekeepers to the maximum 5x bonus rate.

What’s New for 179D in 2025:

The 5X Multiplier: Learn the difference between the base deduction (approx. $0.60–$1.20/sq. ft.) and the bonus deduction (approx. $3.00–$5.80/sq. ft.).

Expanded Eligibility: It’s no longer just for government buildings. Designers can now receive allocations from non-profits, religious organizations, tribal entities, and universities.

Lower Thresholds: The minimum energy reduction required to qualify has been lowered from 50% to 25% (measured against ASHRAE 90.1-2007).

Retrofit Pathway: A new alternative path for existing buildings to qualify based on reduced energy intensity.

The Two Critical Bonus Requirements:

To unlock the 5x bonus rate, projects must comply with two rigorous labor standards:

Prevailing Wage: All laborers and mechanics must be paid at or above the local prevailing rates for their specific classification.

Apprenticeship Standards: Projects must meet "Labor Hour" and "Participation" requirements. Starting in 2024, at least 15% of total labor hours must be performed by qualified apprentices.

metadata.title: How Does Section 179d (aka the "Green Building Tax Deduction") Work?
metadata.author: Rob Freeman | Insuring The Built Environment
metadata.shortDescription:
https://robfreeman.com/ - Section 179d, also known as the "green building" or commercial building energy efficiency deduction, provides a tax deduction of up to $5.00 per square foot for projects placed in service between January 1st, 2023 and December 31st, 2032.

Section 179d was originally introduced as a temporary incentive in the Energy Policy Act of 2005. The green building tax deduction became permanent in 2020 provides and was extended with the IRA.
Tax incentives encourage commercial building owners to make their buildings efficient beyond a baseline standard of energy efficiency established by the American Society of Heating, Refrigeration and Air -Conditioning Engineers (ASHRAE).

ASHRAE 90.1 is the energy standard for sites and buildings, except low-rise residential buildings. The standard is updated regularly and the latest version of the ASHRAE 90.1 standard is 90.1-2022.

For commercial building owners, the base deduction starts at $0.50 cents per square foot for a 25% improvement over the ASHRAE 90.1 energy efficiency baseline. The base deduction can be increased up to $1.00 per square foot for each percentage improvement over the 90.1 baseline, up to 50%.

Bonus deductions are possible, up to as much as $5.00 per square foot by meeting prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements, as described in more detail on the IRS website.

Section 179d may be used by private building owners as well as real estate investment trusts (REITs) and even tax exempt entities. The deduction may be used more than once, meaning that incremental improvements in building systems can be applied approximately every 3 years.

Section 179D Energy Efficient Commercial Buildings Deduction (Section 179D) was significantly enhanced through the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), offering commercial building owners and designers, like architects and engineers, potential lucrative tax credits. metadata.title: The Energy Deduction Commercial Contractors Keep Missing
metadata.author: George Ghazarian, CPA
metadata.shortDescription:
If you’re a construction contractor, GC, mechanical contractor, lighting contractor, architect, engineer, or design-build pro, this episode is a must-watch. Section 179D is one of the most powerful—and underused—tax deductions available for commercial construction and government projects.
In this video, I break down how 179D works, who qualifies, how much money is on the table, and exactly how contractors can claim the deduction (even when the building owner can’t).
________________________________________

🔧 What You’ll Learn in This Episode
👉 What Section 179D Actually Is
179D is an energy-efficient commercial building deduction.
If your work helps a building save energy—through lighting, HVAC, or envelope improvements—the IRS may allow YOU, the designer/contractor, to take the deduction when the owner can’t (government + tax-exempt buildings).
Eligible building owners include:
• Schools & universities
• Airports
• Libraries
• Courthouses
• Military & municipal buildings
• Nonprofits & religious institutions
Eligible “designers” include:
• GCs
• Design-build firms
• Mechanical contractors
• Lighting contractors
• Architects & engineers
• Energy consultants
________________________________________

💰 How Big Is the Deduction?
Depending on energy savings + labor rules, the deduction ranges from:
💵 $0.54 to $5.00+ per square foot
Example:
• A 100,000 sq. ft. school project could generate $54,000 to $500,000+ in tax deductions.
For contractors doing multiple projects per year, this becomes a major tax strategy.
________________________________________

⚡ What Types of Work Qualify?
179D applies to improvements in three core systems:
1. Interior Lighting Systems
LED retrofits, high-efficiency lighting, controls, daylighting.
2. HVAC & Hot Water Systems
VRF systems, chillers, heat pumps, efficient ventilation, boilers.
3. Building Envelope
Insulation, roofing, windows, doors, air sealing.
If your work reduces energy usage, it may qualify.
________________________________________

📄 How to Claim the Deduction (Step-by-Step)
Step 1 — Meet Efficiency Requirements
A licensed third-party engineer calculates energy savings using IRS-approved software.
Step 2 — Get the Allocation Letter
Because the building owner is tax-exempt, they must formally allocate the deduction to you.
This letter must:
• Be signed by the tax-exempt/government owner
• Identify you as the “designer”
• Specify which project elements you’re allocated
No letter = no deduction.
Step 3 — Obtain an Energy Certification
A qualified, independent engineer certifies the results.
Step 4 — Claim on Your Tax Return
Your CPA (that’s me 😄) applies the deduction to your business or personal return.
________________________________________

📈 Recent Changes That Make 179D Even Better
The Inflation Reduction Act expanded 179D by:
✔ Making the deduction permanent
✔ Significantly increasing the dollar amount available
✔ Allowing tax-exempt entities to allocate the deduction to contractors
✔ Enabling deductions to be taken year after year for ongoing improvements
More gov’t + nonprofit projects = more contractor opportunities.
________________________________________

🏗 Real Contractor Examples (Actual Math)
Lighting Contractor — Public School Retrofit
• 90,000 sq. ft.
• Meets prevailing wage
➡️ $450,000 deduction
Mechanical Contractor — City Hall HVAC Upgrade
• 50,000 sq. ft.
➡️ $150,000 deduction
General Contractor — Nonprofit New Construction
• 120,000 sq. ft.
• Lighting + HVAC + envelope
➡️ $600,000+ deduction
These offsets can reduce:
• Corporate tax
• Personal income tax
• Capital gains
• In some cases, AMT
________________________________________

🧰 How Contractors Maximize 179D
1. Identify qualifying projects early (ask during bid stage)
2. Meet prevailing wage & apprenticeship rules for higher deduction
3. Line up your third-party engineer early
4. Secure the allocation letter BEFORE filing
5. Work with a CPA who specializes in construction tax incentives
________________________________________

🎬 Closing Thoughts
Section 179D is one of the best, most powerful tax tools available to contractors working on:
• Government buildings
• Schools
• Universities
• Airports
• Hospitals
• Nonprofits
• Commercial buildings with energy upgrades
If you’re not using it, you’re likely leaving serious money on the table.
________________________________________

🔗 Connect with Us 
• 🌐 accountingsolutionsllp.com   
• 💼 LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/george-ghazarian-asllp/   
• Book a Strategy Call: https://accountingsolutionsllp.com/appointment/

Disclaimer: This content is provided for educational purposes only and is not legal, tax, accounting, or financial advice. Every situation is unique, so consult your own attorney, CPA, or financial advisor before making decisions based on this information.
